title: Legion, a Bleeding Woman, and Jairus's Daughter
summary: Across the lake in Gentile territory, Jesus frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, who enter a herd of pigs that rush into the sea; the frightened townspeople ask Jesus to leave, and the healed man proclaims what Jesus has done throughout the Decapolis. Back on the Jewish side, Jairus begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak and is healed, and though word comes that the girl has died, Jesus takes her by the hand and raises her to life.
story: At the end of chapter 4 the disciples asked who Jesus is, since even wind and sea obey him. Chapter 5 answers with three more displays of his authority, each over a power more desperate than the last: a host of demons, a chronic disease that no doctor could cure, and death itself. The storm on the lake gives way to a different kind of chaos in a man living among tombs. Together with the storm, these stories form a sequence of four mighty works that show the reach of God's kingdom in Jesus. They also set up the contrast of chapter 6, where Jesus' hometown refuses to believe and he can do few mighty works there.
historical:
The eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee was largely Gentile territory, part of the region of the Decapolis, a loose group of ten cities with Greek culture and Roman oversight, most lying east of the Jordan. Keeping pigs, which Jewish law treated as unclean (Leviticus 11:7), was normal there. Ancient manuscripts differ over the region's name, reading Gerasenes, Gadarenes, or Gergesenes. The city of Gerasa lay about thirty miles southeast of the lake, and Gadara about six miles away, so the name may refer broadly to the territory of a city rather than the town itself. Many scholars locate the event near Kursi on the eastern shore, where there is a steep slope near the water and where a large Byzantine monastery later commemorated the miracle.

The word Legion would have meant one thing to anyone in the Roman east: a unit of the Roman army of several thousand soldiers, the visible face of imperial power. Some interpreters see an intended echo of Roman occupation in the story, especially since a legion stationed in the region in later decades, the Tenth, used a boar among its emblems; others think the name simply conveys overwhelming numbers. Jairus, by contrast, belongs to the Jewish side of the lake, a synagogue leader responsible for arranging the services and caring for the building, a respected man in his town.
cultural:
Tombs were often caves or chambers cut into hillsides, places of ritual impurity that respectable people avoided, and the possessed man's life there shows how completely he had been cut off from community. Unclean spirit, tombs, and pigs together make a picture of total uncleanness from a Jewish point of view, and Jesus enters it. The woman's condition also made her ritually unclean under the law (Leviticus 15:25-27), and anyone she touched became unclean until evening. For twelve years she would have been kept from much of ordinary worship and social life, and Mark adds that she had spent all she had on doctors who made her worse.

Mourning in Jewish households began immediately after a death, with loud wailing and often hired mourners and flute players; later Jewish law expected even a poor family to hire at least a few for a funeral. The mourners' scorn at Jesus' words shows the girl was plainly dead. Talitha koum is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jewish Palestine, and Mark keeps the words and translates them for his Greek-speaking readers. Calling the woman daughter gave her public standing and restored her to the community in front of the crowd.
literary: The chapter has two main episodes, and the second is one of Mark's sandwich stories: the raising of Jairus's daughter (verses 21 to 24 and 35 to 43) is interrupted by the healing of the bleeding woman (25 to 34). The two stories are deliberately linked. Both involve a daughter, both involve the number twelve (years of illness, years of age), both involve touch and uncleanness, and both are about faith in the face of hopelessness. The delay caused by the woman seems to cost Jairus his daughter, which heightens the tension, and Jesus' word to him, “Do not be afraid; just believe,” carries the lesson of the first story into the second. The Gerasene story is told with vivid detail and ends with a commission: the healed man becomes the first person Jesus sends to tell others about him.

outline.t: A man possessed by Legion set free
The townspeople's fear and the healed man's witness
A woman healed by touching Jesus' cloak

doctrines.note: The same Greek word means to heal and to save, and Mark uses it for the woman's healing and for Jairus's hope for his daughter. Jesus' rescue reaches the whole person: body, mind, social standing, and relationship with God.

The woman's faith is imperfect and almost superstitious, and Jairus's faith is shaken by news of death, yet Jesus honors both. Faith in Mark is reaching out to Jesus in need and continuing to trust him when circumstances say it is too late.

Jesus calls death sleep, not because the girl was not dead but because for him death is not final. Raising her anticipates his own resurrection and the resurrection of the dead that Christians confess.

words.note: Sozo, to save, rescue, heal, or make whole. Jairus asks that his daughter be healed, using this word, and the woman believes that touching Jesus will make her well. Jesus tells her that her faith has healed her. The word bridges physical healing and the fuller salvation Jesus brings.

Legion, a Latin military term borrowed into Greek, meaning a Roman army unit of several thousand soldiers. As a name for the spirits it conveys a vast, organized, oppressive force, and it makes the man's rescue all the more striking: one word from Jesus is stronger than an army.

Pistis, faith or trust. Jesus tells the woman that her faith has healed her, directing attention away from the cloak to her trust in him. Faith is not a power in itself but reliance on Jesus, which is why he insists on meeting her face to face.

Koum, an Aramaic word meaning get up or arise, transliterated into Greek. It is one of several places where Mark preserves the very sound of Jesus' words, giving readers a sense of eyewitness memory and of the simplicity of the command that raised the dead.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as Lord over every power that destroys human life. The demons call him Son of the Most High God and beg him not to torment them, recognizing their judge. When the healed man is told to proclaim how much the Lord has done for him, he goes and proclaims how much Jesus has done, which quietly identifies Jesus with the Lord. Jesus is not made unclean by tombs, pigs, bleeding, or death; instead, his holiness and life flow outward and make the unclean clean and the dead alive. For Mark's readers, who knew of his cross and empty tomb, the raising of a twelve-year-old girl anticipates what God would do for Jesus himself.

hard.q: How should a modern reader understand demon possession, and why did Jesus allow the pigs to be destroyed?
hard.a:
Many readers today assume that what the Gospels call possession was mental illness or epilepsy described in ancient terms. The Gospels themselves distinguish between ordinary illness and possession (Mark 1:32-34), and many Christians around the world, and many who work with severe spiritual oppression, hold that evil spiritual powers are real, as the whole New Testament assumes. Others think both descriptions can be true at once, since spiritual and physical realities overlap. What the story plainly shows is a man destroyed by forces beyond his control, and Jesus restoring him to his right mind.

The loss of two thousand pigs troubles readers as a destruction of animals and of the owners' livelihood. Some note that the demons, not Jesus, drive the herd to destruction, and that Jesus permits it, showing visibly that they had left the man and revealing their destructive nature. Others see it as a sign that one human life is worth more than a whole herd, something the townspeople could not accept, since they asked Jesus to leave instead of rejoicing over the man. The text does not fully explain Jesus' permission, and honest readers can acknowledge the difficulty while noticing the story's point: the townspeople feared Jesus' power more than they valued the healing of their neighbor.

questions: The healed man wanted to go with Jesus, but Jesus sent him home to tell his own people. Where might Jesus be sending you to tell what he has done?
The woman tried to be healed secretly, but Jesus called her forward and named her daughter. Why do you think he insisted on meeting her?
Jesus told Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe,” right after hearing that his daughter had died. What situation in your life needs that word?
